title: The US Treasury Secretary Threatens Allies with Divine Wrath, Proving He Has No Cards
dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent portrays America as an irritable god and demands allies submit like Pascal's wager. Farrell sees through this op-ed: the louder the threat, the more it proves the US lacks the means to deliver, and allies have already begun to fend for themselves.
why: A counter-reading of a seemingly tough Treasury op-ed: theological intimidation mostly goes unfulfilled, and understanding this lets you predict allies' real hand in trade negotiations.
who: Decision-makers doing cross-border business, investors watching dollar assets and tariff risks, and policy researchers trying to judge whether allies will cave.
skip: Skip the first 4 minutes of intro and subscription prompts; start directly with the Carney speech and the Bessent op-ed.

points.h: The Treasury Secretary Casts America as an Angry God
points.body: In his "Economic D-Day" op-ed in the Financial Times, Bessent packaged the choice facing allies as Pascal's wager. Farrell's dissection: he is effectively saying you must treat America as God, appease this irritable deity by any means, or it will strike you with lightning. Farrell describes it as a 17th-century Puritan sermon, one that could be retitled "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God," except the sinners are the rest of the world. The problem is that this kind of sermonizing is usually the reaction of a preacher who sees his congregation leaving, not a sign of strength.

points.h: The Louder the Shout, the Softer the Stick
points.body: Roosevelt's famous line was "speak softly and carry a big stick." Farrell says Bessent's approach is the reverse: speak bigly and carry a soft stick. The real test is China: China is currently the country most capable of supporting Iran, and Bessent simply does not want to answer whether the US would dare bring its wrath down on China if it keeps buying Iranian oil. Farrell thinks markets and nations are all betting it won't. So the op-ed reads more like an empty threat: the more absolute the language, the more it looks like America bluffing at an empty table.

points.h: Flexible Realism Equals No Strategy at All
points.body: Using "flexible realism" to explain White House behavior is throwing a cloth over chaos. Farrell says that once you unpack the term, it amounts to one sentence: America does whatever it wants, and other countries had better adjust themselves to it. What actually makes the White House run is not strategy but a contest for attention, like Cosimo de' Medici making everyone revolve around him—except Trump does "a stupid version": as long as he can be the center of everyone's attention, he can make decisions that are extremely stupid in both the long and short term. Other countries' response therefore becomes damage limitation, not continuing to bet.

points.h: The Mechanism of Ambition Counteracting Ambition Has Failed
points.body: Federalist No. 10 offered the answer of "ambition counteracting ambition": let each person's drive for power cancel out others', grinding toward an equilibrium close to the public interest. Farrell says this mechanism has been dismantled from both ends. One end is the Republican Party: internal dissent has almost vanished, senators who disagree dare not publicly block, and one-party control of all three branches short-circuits the old checks. The other end is federal agencies: the Supreme Court embraces the "unitary executive" theory, inspectors general are fired or intimidated, and ordinary civil servants are converted into at-will employees who can be dismissed at any time. With a wholly unqualified person at the top of the system, mistakes get amplified into nationwide madness.

points.h: Rebuilding American Institutions Requires Learning to Experiment
points.body: Farrell does not think institutions can return to the old consensus of the early 1990s to 2015, but he also does not think America is doomed to slide into disaster. The model he favors is the experiment New York Mayor Mamdani is running: building a feedback loop between city government and the public, turning people's real troubles into policy, and using social media to let the public see "I'm listening, and I'm doing." He deliberately links this style to Roosevelt's "bold, persistent experimentation": keep what works, throw out what doesn't. The real open question is whether America's media and political system can tolerate a politician openly saying "this path didn't work, let's try another"—without that tolerance, experimentation won't go far.

points.h: The More Flexible, the Less Anyone Takes You Seriously
points.body: The biggest problem with flexible realism is that it destroys an asset that depletes with fickleness—credibility. Farrell cites Nobel economics laureate Thomas Schelling's argument: one of a nation's most important assets is credibility; promises and threats that can be delivered are what actually work in negotiations. If you change your mind at any moment, and a threat you swore by the day before yesterday vanishes the next day, then at a certain point no one takes you seriously anymore. Farrell thinks America is in this state today: other countries still fear its capacity to do harm, but no longer believe it has the capacity for long-term action. His image: a drunk grandfather holding a shotgun, and everyone just humors him so he won't fire.

points.h: America Is Smashing Its Own Web with a Sledgehammer
points.body: The core question in Farrell and Newman's Underground Empire is: globalization is a web of interdependence—supply chains interlock across dozens of countries and thousands of suppliers, and dollar clearing is the nervous system of this network. America built this system with one hand and reserved "house advantage" for itself with the other, using the threat of cutting off network access to constrain others. The Trump administration's current approach is not to delicately dismantle the web but to swing a sledgehammer semi-randomly at various parts. Farrell's direction is clear: complete decoupling from one another would be a disaster; what countries can do is not become independent, but make interdependence resilient, while getting major powers to relearn the language of "restraint."

points.h: One Rare Earth Card Punctures the Invincibility Narrative
points.body: On last year's "tariff big day," Bessent publicly said America held all A's and China had no cards. Weeks later China played the rare earths and critical minerals card, and America suddenly realized it was holding a busted flush—a hand that looked fierce but never came together. Farrell sees this as the key moment that sobered the US side; since then, in speeches by Marco Rubio and others, you can see this recognition: China has the ability to materially hurt the US economy. The US and China now live in a fragile balance where each knows "I can cripple you," but they have not yet truly sat down to negotiate that balance into more stable rules.
